description:
We are a group of curious minds from  Pearl of Africa (Uganda) that  teamed up to build app  that turning free NASA data into simple crop rotation advice for poor farmers the CROPSAT 
It  gives farmers free, satellite-based guidance on erosion, soil fertility, water, climate risk and crop order, in plain language. It helps most when used together with local extension advice in crop rotation and others
summary:
We developed CROPSAT , a web app that helps farmers plan crop rotations using NASA data. A farmer taps any field on a satellite map, or picks a regional preset, and the app pulls live NASA POWER climate data and SRTM elevation data for that spot. It combines this with what the farmer know ie he can adjust  to what he knows soil pH, altitude, soil texture, current crops and priorities. The app then shows "Bare-Soil Danger Windows", the months when heavy rain hits uncovered soil after harvest. A two-stage Google Gemini AI co-pilot asks 3 questions that satellites cannot answer, then creates 3 twelve-month crop rotation strategies. Heat and rainfall sliders let users test each plan against climate shocks.
This addresses the Field Shift challenge by turning NASA Earth observations into practical farm decisions. It matters because soil erosion, poor soil fertility unpredictable weather threaten food security especially for smallholder farmers who cannot afford sensors or advisers. The tool supports and never replaces, local extension advice.
details:
What it does and how it works
CROP SAT is a web app that turns NASA satellite and climate data into crop rotation advice for a specific field. It works in four steps:
Field and ground-truth input. The user taps a point on a satellite map (Esri World Imagery) or picks a preset: Wakiso (Uganda), Mt. Elgon (Uganda), Machakos (Kenya) or Central Valley (California). They then enter elevation, soil pH, soil texture, current crops and priorities. The app warns about nutrient problems, such as phosphorus lock-up in acidic soil.
NASA data scan. The app queries NASA POWER climate data, SRTM elevation and ISRIC SoilGrids soil data at the same time. It shows four indicators (soil moisture, heat stress, rainfall and frost risk, erosion risk) and a 12-month chart. Months with low vegetation cover (NDVI below 0.30) and heavy rain (80 mm or more) are marked as Bare-Soil Danger Windows.
Calibration. A Google Gemini AI co-pilot asks 3 questions that satellites cannot answer such as residue management or access to lime.
Strategies and stress test. The AI creates 3 rotation plans: baseline, soil-regenerative, and climate-adaptive cash crops. Each plan has a 12-month timeline , impact scores and an Extension Review checklist. Heat (0 to +4°C) and rainfall (-40% to +30%) sliders show how each plan holds up.
Benefits and intended impact
Reduces topsoil loss by showing when to keep the ground covered.
Improves soil fertilityfor example by matching legumes to soil pH so they fix nitrogen.
Helps farmers without sensors or weather stations plan for climate change.
Supports local extension officers instead of replacing them because every plan lists what satellites cannot verify (for example plow pans, seed supply and market prices).
Tools and technology
Frontend: React 19, TypeScript, Vite, Tailwind CSS, Leaflet and React Leaflet.
Backend and testing: Node.js, Express, Node's built-in test runner.
AI: Google AI Studio and the Google GenAI SDK, running on the server with structured JSON output.
Data: NASA POWER, Open-Elevation (SRTM), ISRIC SoilGrids
Hardware: none special; it runs in a normal web browser.
What make it creative
It admits that satellite pixels (9 km to 300 km) are much coarser than a 1 m field, and fixes this by asking the farmer 3 questions.
It combines data at many scales in one screen.
It has a Farmer Plain-Language mode and a NASA Scientist mode.
It falls back to regional profiles and a rule-based engine if internet or AI fails.
Factors considered
Smallholder farmers, poor connectivity, safety (AI suggestions are checked by extension officers) nd clear labelling of live data versus modelled estimates.
